rules.quote: The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters.
rules.specification: The maximum is explicit, but the page does not specify how to count links, emoji or other characters that the platform may weight specially.
rules.violation_condition: A tweet exceeds the stated maximum of 280 characters.
when: Applies to tweets on X (formerly Twitter), as described on this page.
rules.why: The stated maximum is a checkable constraint, not merely a description of typical tweet length.

rules.quote: Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence.
rules.specification: The single-idea, single-sentence structure is explicit. The page supplies no length threshold for ‘short’ or operational test for ‘attention-grabbing’.
rules.violation_condition: A tweet does not express one idea in a single short, attention-grabbing sentence.
when: Applies to tweets on X (formerly Twitter).
rules.why: One coherent check of the prescribed tweet structure; no numerical brevity threshold is invented (E-4).

rules.quote: Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.
rules.violation_condition: A government tweet contains internet slang.
when: Applies to government tweets on X (formerly Twitter).
rules.why: Slang is a distinct lexical violation, separate from tweet length and structure.

rules.quote: Use keywords in hashtags, which have a # symbol.
rules.specification: Topic relevance is inferred from the explanation about finding and following topics. The page does not otherwise define which terms qualify as keywords.
rules.violation_condition: A hashtag does not use keywords relevant to the post’s topic.
when: Applies when hashtags are used in posts on X (formerly Twitter).
rules.why: The instruction concerns hashtag wording; the explanatory definition of the # symbol is not made into another rule.

rules.quote: If you are publishing a new topic, try to use an existing or trending hashtag rather than creating a new one.
rules.specification: Checking requires external information about existing or trending hashtags. The page does not specify a source, time window or test of whether an existing hashtag is applicable.
rules.violation_condition: A post introducing a new topic creates a hashtag instead of using an applicable existing or trending hashtag.
when: Applies to posts on X (formerly Twitter) publishing a new topic.
The preference can only be assessed where an applicable existing or trending hashtag is available.
rules.why: The named alternatives establish a preference; the new-topic condition stays within the rule (G-2).

rules.quote: You need no more than 2 hashtags.
rules.violation_condition: A post contains more than 2 hashtags.
when: Applies to posts on X (formerly Twitter).
This is an upper limit, not a requirement to include hashtags.
rules.why: One hashtag-count check; the explanation about readability does not create another rule.

covers.quote: The first letter of each word in the hashtag starts with a capital letter – for example, #SelfQuarantine.

examples.note: The example is embedded in explanatory prose.

rules.quote: Use ‘camel case’ for compound hashtags.
rules.violation_condition: A compound hashtag has a constituent word whose first letter is not capitalised.
when: Applies to compound hashtags in posts on X (formerly Twitter).
The page defines its use of ‘camel case’ as capitalising the first letter of every word, including the first word.
rules.why: The body defines the heading terminology; it is part of the same capitalisation check (G-4).

rules.quote: Address other users with the @ sign before their username.
rules.violation_condition: A post addresses another user by username without an immediately preceding @ sign.
when: Applies when addressing another user by username on X (formerly Twitter).
Does not require every reference to a person to be a username mention.
rules.why: The missing mention marker is a textual violation; the reminder that tweets are public is advice.

rules.quote: Do not publish technical content on Facebook.
rules.specification: The page does not define ‘technical content’ or provide examples establishing its boundary. Do not reduce this to a jargon-only check.
rules.violation_condition: A Facebook post contains technical content.
when: Applies to Facebook posts.
rules.why: This is a platform-specific restriction on content, not merely a description of Facebook’s uses.

rules.quote: Content needs to be compelling so it reaches the people you want to reach.
rules.specification: The page supplies no operational test for compelling content. Its observation about scrolling within 2 seconds is not a measurable reading-time requirement.
rules.violation_condition: The text of a Facebook post is not compelling to its intended audience.
when: Applies to Facebook post text.
Assessment requires the intended audience.
rules.why: The body states a property of content; the preceding attention-span observation is not a separate rule.

rules.quote: include a compelling title
rules.specification: Title presence is directly checkable, but the page gives no operational test for a compelling title.
rules.violation_condition: A YouTube video has no title, or its title is not compelling.
when: Applies to titles of YouTube videos.
rules.why: G-1: mark the textual child requirement, not the lead-in or the non-text production requirements.

rules.quote: Include all your information in the post rather than linking to websites.
rules.violation_condition: An Instagram post depends on a website link for information instead of including that information in the post.
when: Applies to Instagram posts.
rules.why: The named alternatives concern self-contained post information versus sending users to a website.

rules.quote: Use plain language
rules.specification: Avoiding jargon and acronyms is explicit. The page does not specify a broader readability test or reading level for plain language.
rules.violation_condition: A social-media post uses language its audience cannot readily understand, including jargon or acronyms.
when: Applies across social-media platforms.
Assess comprehensibility for the intended audience.
rules.why: The explicit lexical guidance is consolidated into the plain-language check to avoid flagging jargon twice.

rules.quote: Use plain language and a conversational, positive tone on social media.
rules.violation_condition: A social-media post has a tone that is not conversational and positive.
when: Applies across social-media platforms.
rules.why: Tone is distinct from comprehensibility. This item checks only the conversational, positive tone clause.

rules.quote: Don’t add a full stop after hashtags, emojis or handles.
rules.violation_condition: A full stop follows a hashtag, emoji or handle.
when: Applies across social-media platforms.
The prohibition is specifically on full stops; it does not prohibit question marks or exclamation marks.
rules.why: The three preceding element types are cases of the same punctuation violation (G-2).

rules.quote: Use them sparingly.
rules.specification: ‘Them’ refers to emojis. The page does not define ‘sparingly’; no numerical emoji limit is supplied.
rules.violation_condition: A social-media post uses emojis excessively.
when: Applies when a social-media post uses emojis.
rules.why: Emoji frequency is a property of the post; following an organisation’s guidelines is separate writer advice (G-5).

covers.quote: Emojis are standardised pictographs. Emoticons display as punctuation marks in text and are not standardised.

rules.quote: Use emojis, not emoticons.
rules.violation_condition: A social-media post uses punctuation-based emoticons instead of emojis.
when: Applies when choosing between emojis and emoticons.
Does not require a post to contain either.
rules.why: The named alternatives form one preference; the following definitions explain the distinction.

rules.quote: Choose common emojis
rules.specification: The page does not identify a list of common emojis, a frequency threshold or the population against which commonness is assessed.
rules.violation_condition: A social-media post uses an uncommon emoji.
when: Applies when emojis are used.
rules.why: Emoji familiarity is separate from whether the message remains understandable without the emoji.

rules.quote: make sure the user can understand the message if the emoji is removed.
rules.violation_condition: Removing an emoji leaves the post’s message incomplete or not understandable.
when: Applies to posts containing emojis.
rules.why: This is a textual meaning check, distinct from emoji choice and frequency.

covers.quote: Use inclusive imagery and inclusive language.

rules.quote: Content needs respect all people, their rights and their heritage.
rules.violation_condition: A post’s wording is disrespectful of people, their rights or heritage, or uses non-inclusive language.
when: Applies across social-media platforms.
This check concerns language, not the inclusivity of images.
rules.why: Respectful, inclusive wording is one textual check; the imagery component is excluded as not_text.

rules.quote: Use alt text and closed captions, or provide a link to content with these elements.
rules.violation_condition: A post’s image lacks alt text, or its video lacks closed captions, and no link to content providing the required text alternative is supplied.
when: Alt text applies to images and closed captions to video.
A link to content with these elements is an allowed alternative.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: media type changes the required text alternative, and the linked-content alternative stays within this rule. G-4 consolidates the repeated alt-text instruction.

rules.quote: Also ensure you include any text in the image that is in the text of the post itself.
rules.specification: Interpret this as requiring text embedded in an image to also appear in the post text. The source wording appears to reverse or muddle that relationship; the reviewer should confirm this interpretation.
rules.violation_condition: Information expressed as text within an image is missing from the text of the social-media post.
when: Applies to posts containing images with text.
rules.why: This is a separate text-equivalence check, not merely the presence of alt text. The uncertain wording is exposed rather than silently corrected.

rules.quote: You must attribute copyright material.
rules.violation_condition: Copyright material used in a post has no attribution.
when: Applies when a post uses copyright material, including video and images.
rules.why: Attribution is a required textual element. Obtaining a licence is a separate publishing process, not an observable textual property.

rules.quote: Be specific so the context is clear from the post itself.
rules.violation_condition: A post omits the specific information needed to understand its intended message without surrounding context.
when: Assess the post on its own, including when it is shared outside its original context.
rules.why: The body states a checkable property of the post; the preceding instruction to think carefully is writer advice (G-5).

anchor.quote: The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters.
anchor.suffix: Write one idea in a short, atte

tags.specification: The maximum is explicit, but the page does not specify how to count links, emoji or other characters that the platform may weight specially.
tags.violation_condition: A tweet exceeds the stated maximum of 280 characters.

when: Applies to tweets on X (formerly Twitter), as described on this page.
rules.why: The stated maximum is a checkable constraint, not merely a description of typical tweet length.

anchor.quote: Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence.
anchor.suffix: Most tweets have a key idea and

tags.specification: The single-idea, single-sentence structure is explicit. The page supplies no length threshold for ‘short’ or operational test for ‘attention-grabbing’.
tags.violation_condition: A tweet does not express one idea in a single short, attention-grabbing sentence.

when: Applies to tweets on X (formerly Twitter).
rules.why: One coherent check of the prescribed tweet structure; no numerical brevity threshold is invented (E-4).

anchor.prefix: y idea and a link to a webpage.
anchor.quote: Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

tags.violation_condition: A government tweet contains internet slang.

when: Applies to government tweets on X (formerly Twitter).
rules.why: Slang is a distinct lexical violation, separate from tweet length and structure.

anchor.quote: Use keywords in hashtags, which have a # symbol.
anchor.suffix: Hashtags help people find and f

tags.specification: Topic relevance is inferred from the explanation about finding and following topics. The page does not otherwise define which terms qualify as keywords.
tags.violation_condition: A hashtag does not use keywords relevant to the post’s topic.

when: Applies when hashtags are used in posts on X (formerly Twitter).
rules.why: The instruction concerns hashtag wording; the explanatory definition of the # symbol is not made into another rule.

anchor.quote: If you are publishing a new topic, try to use an existing or trending hashtag rather than creating a new one.

tags.specification: Checking requires external information about existing or trending hashtags. The page does not specify a source, time window or test of whether an existing hashtag is applicable.
tags.violation_condition: A post introducing a new topic creates a hashtag instead of using an applicable existing or trending hashtag.

when: Applies to posts on X (formerly Twitter) publishing a new topic.
The preference can only be assessed where an applicable existing or trending hashtag is available.
rules.why: The named alternatives establish a preference; the new-topic condition stays within the rule (G-2).

anchor.quote: You need no more than 2 hashtags.
anchor.suffix: Too many hashtags makes your co

tags.violation_condition: A post contains more than 2 hashtags.

when: Applies to posts on X (formerly Twitter).
This is an upper limit, not a requirement to include hashtags.
rules.why: One hashtag-count check; the explanation about readability does not create another rule.

anchor.quote: Use ‘camel case’ for compound hashtags.
anchor.suffix: The first letter of each word i

covers.quote: The first letter of each word in the hashtag starts with a capital letter – for example, #SelfQuarantine.

examples.note: The example is embedded in explanatory prose.

tags.violation_condition: A compound hashtag has a constituent word whose first letter is not capitalised.

when: Applies to compound hashtags in posts on X (formerly Twitter).
The page defines its use of ‘camel case’ as capitalising the first letter of every word, including the first word.
rules.why: The body defines the heading terminology; it is part of the same capitalisation check (G-4).

anchor.quote: Address other users with the @ sign before their username.

tags.violation_condition: A post addresses another user by username without an immediately preceding @ sign.

when: Applies when addressing another user by username on X (formerly Twitter).
Does not require every reference to a person to be a username mention.
rules.why: The missing mention marker is a textual violation; the reminder that tweets are public is advice.

anchor.quote: Do not publish technical content on Facebook.

tags.specification: The page does not define ‘technical content’ or provide examples establishing its boundary. Do not reduce this to a jargon-only check.
tags.violation_condition: A Facebook post contains technical content.

when: Applies to Facebook posts.
rules.why: This is a platform-specific restriction on content, not merely a description of Facebook’s uses.

anchor.prefix: past it, if they see it at all.
anchor.quote: Content needs to be compelling so it reaches the people you want to reach.

tags.specification: The page supplies no operational test for compelling content. Its observation about scrolling within 2 seconds is not a measurable reading-time requirement.
tags.violation_condition: The text of a Facebook post is not compelling to its intended audience.

when: Applies to Facebook post text.
Assessment requires the intended audience.
rules.why: The body states a property of content; the preceding attention-span observation is not a separate rule.

anchor.quote: include a compelling title

tags.specification: Title presence is directly checkable, but the page gives no operational test for a compelling title.
tags.violation_condition: A YouTube video has no title, or its title is not compelling.

when: Applies to titles of YouTube videos.
rules.why: G-1: mark the textual child requirement, not the lead-in or the non-text production requirements.

anchor.prefix: s don’t work well on Instagram.
anchor.quote: Include all your information in the post rather than linking to websites.

tags.violation_condition: An Instagram post depends on a website link for information instead of including that information in the post.

when: Applies to Instagram posts.
rules.why: The named alternatives concern self-contained post information versus sending users to a website.

anchor.quote: Use plain language

tags.specification: Avoiding jargon and acronyms is explicit. The page does not specify a broader readability test or reading level for plain language.
tags.violation_condition: A social-media post uses language its audience cannot readily understand, including jargon or acronyms.

when: Applies across social-media platforms.
Assess comprehensibility for the intended audience.
rules.why: The explicit lexical guidance is consolidated into the plain-language check to avoid flagging jargon twice.

anchor.quote: Use plain language and a conversational, positive tone on social media.

tags.violation_condition: A social-media post has a tone that is not conversational and positive.

when: Applies across social-media platforms.
rules.why: Tone is distinct from comprehensibility. This item checks only the conversational, positive tone clause.

anchor.quote: Don’t add a full stop after hashtags, emojis or handles.

tags.violation_condition: A full stop follows a hashtag, emoji or handle.

when: Applies across social-media platforms.
The prohibition is specifically on full stops; it does not prohibit question marks or exclamation marks.
rules.why: The three preceding element types are cases of the same punctuation violation (G-2).

anchor.quote: Use them sparingly.

tags.specification: ‘Them’ refers to emojis. The page does not define ‘sparingly’; no numerical emoji limit is supplied.
tags.violation_condition: A social-media post uses emojis excessively.

when: Applies when a social-media post uses emojis.
rules.why: Emoji frequency is a property of the post; following an organisation’s guidelines is separate writer advice (G-5).

anchor.quote: Use emojis, not emoticons.

covers.quote: Emojis are standardised pictographs. Emoticons display as punctuation marks in text and are not standardised.

tags.violation_condition: A social-media post uses punctuation-based emoticons instead of emojis.

when: Applies when choosing between emojis and emoticons.
Does not require a post to contain either.
rules.why: The named alternatives form one preference; the following definitions explain the distinction.

anchor.quote: Choose common emojis
anchor.suffix: and make sure the user can unde

tags.specification: The page does not identify a list of common emojis, a frequency threshold or the population against which commonness is assessed.
tags.violation_condition: A social-media post uses an uncommon emoji.

when: Applies when emojis are used.
rules.why: Emoji familiarity is separate from whether the message remains understandable without the emoji.

anchor.quote: make sure the user can understand the message if the emoji is removed.

tags.violation_condition: Removing an emoji leaves the post’s message incomplete or not understandable.

when: Applies to posts containing emojis.
rules.why: This is a textual meaning check, distinct from emoji choice and frequency.

anchor.quote: Content needs respect all people, their rights and their heritage.

covers.quote: Use inclusive imagery and inclusive language.

tags.violation_condition: A post’s wording is disrespectful of people, their rights or heritage, or uses non-inclusive language.

when: Applies across social-media platforms.
This check concerns language, not the inclusivity of images.
rules.why: Respectful, inclusive wording is one textual check; the imagery component is excluded as not_text.

anchor.quote: Use alt text and closed captions, or provide a link to content with these elements.
anchor.suffix: Also ensure you include any tex

tags.violation_condition: A post’s image lacks alt text, or its video lacks closed captions, and no link to content providing the required text alternative is supplied.

when: Alt text applies to images and closed captions to video.
A link to content with these elements is an allowed alternative.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: media type changes the required text alternative, and the linked-content alternative stays within this rule. G-4 consolidates the repeated alt-text instruction.

anchor.quote: Also ensure you include any text in the image that is in the text of the post itself.

tags.specification: Interpret this as requiring text embedded in an image to also appear in the post text. The source wording appears to reverse or muddle that relationship; the reviewer should confirm this interpretation.
tags.violation_condition: Information expressed as text within an image is missing from the text of the social-media post.

when: Applies to posts containing images with text.
rules.why: This is a separate text-equivalence check, not merely the presence of alt text. The uncertain wording is exposed rather than silently corrected.

rules.why: Attribution is a required textual element. Obtaining a licence is a separate publishing process, not an observable textual property.
